The rainwater plan for Chandanpur Girls' School was Rekha's. She had measured the roof in April with a borrowed tape, drawn the tank on graph paper, and handed it to Hansa-ji, the senior teacher, for comments.
At the block education meeting in June, Hansa-ji stood up with the same graph paper, redrawn neatly. "I prepared this plan for our school." The block officer clapped.
Rekha felt heat rush to her face. Was she sure? Yes, the tank was drawn exactly where she had drawn it. But Hansa-ji was senior, and everyone would think Rekha was petty over a drawing. She stared at her tea and said nothing.
In August, Rekha shared her idea for a library corner. At the next meeting, Hansa-ji presented that too.
This time Hansa-ji didn't even glance at her. Rekha understood that her silence in June had been taken as a yes.

qa.q: What did Rekha use to measure the roof?
qa.a: Rekha used a borrowed tape to measure the roof in April.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling at the June meeting?
qa.a: Rekha felt anger rushing to her face, a flicker of doubt, and fear of looking petty in front of a senior teacher.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could Rekha have done in June?
qa.a: Staying silent let it happen again; Rekha could have kept her April drawing and calmly spoken to Hansa-ji or the block officer afterwards.

qa.q: How might Hansa-ji have read Rekha's silence?
qa.a: Hansa-ji seems to have taken it as permission, since in August she presented Rekha's next idea without even glancing at her.

grounding: Rekha sees her rainwater plan presented under a senior's name, stays silent out of doubt and fear of seeming petty, and finds her silence read as consent.

Subject: Need your advice
Hi Sabina,
You were my first manager, so you're the person I trust to tell me if I'm overreacting.
Yesterday Pranay presented the warehouse dashboard to the regional heads. It's my dashboard. My colour scheme, my late-delivery flag, even the typo in the legend I never fixed. He said, "I built this over the weekend."
My face burned. I wanted to stand up. Then I thought: will they think I'm petty? Maybe I shared it with him too casually. Maybe it doesn't count.
So I said nothing. And this is the second time. In March he used my vendor checklist, and when I stayed quiet, he seemed to take that as a yes.
I don't want a fight. I just want my name back on my work.
Can we talk this week?
Madhav

qa.a: Even the typo in the legend that Madhav never fixed.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling during the presentation?
qa.a: Madhav felt angry, face burning, but also doubtful and afraid of seeming petty, so Madhav said nothing.

qa.q: What could Madhav do now so the pattern stops?
qa.a: Talk it through with Sabina, then calmly tell Pranay and the regional heads, with the file history, that the dashboard is Madhav's work.

qa.q: How might Pranay read Madhav's silence?
qa.a: Pranay seems to have taken the earlier silence as a yes, which is why the credit-taking happened a second time.

grounding: Shows an employee finding their dashboard in a colleague's presentation, torn between anger and fear of seeming petty, after silence let it happen again.

You know what happened on Friday, Madhav? I'll tell you, because I haven't told anyone and it's eating me.
So I'm Lokesh, right, the quiet one in the design team. Three weeks ago I sketched a new onboarding screen for the app, the one with the little map. I sent it to Kritika for feedback. On Friday, at the all-hands, there it is on the big screen. Same map. Her name in the corner.
My hands went cold. Everyone clapped. I clapped too. Can you believe that? I clapped.
All weekend I've been going round in circles. Maybe it's normal, maybe designers borrow. Maybe if I say something I'll look small, like I'm counting crumbs. But if I don't, next time she'll do it again, and everyone will think that's just how it is.
So on Monday I'm sending her the original file with the date and asking to talk. Just that. You'll ask me on Tuesday if I did it, okay?

qa.a: Lokesh sent the sketch of a new onboarding screen, the one with the little map, for feedback.

qa.a: Lokesh was shocked, hands cold, and afraid of looking small, so clapping felt safer than speaking up in that moment.

qa.a: Sending Kritika the original dated file and asking to talk on Monday; it is calm and factual, and stops silence from looking like consent.

Monday: In the quarterly review, Harish saw his customer-survey analysis on Jahnavi's slides, word for word, under her name. His neck went hot. He told himself it was a misunderstanding and said nothing.
Friday: The weekly email from Jahnavi went to the whole floor: "Sharing my survey findings again for anyone who missed them." Their manager replied, "Great work, Jahnavi. Can you lead the next survey too?" Harish stared at the screen. His silence had turned into her project.
The following Wednesday: Harish booked fifteen minutes with Jahnavi and their manager. He brought his draft with its timestamps and spoke slowly. "I wrote this analysis. I'd like that to be clear, and I'd like to lead the next survey." Jahnavi went pink and said she'd thought it was "shared material". The manager studied the timestamps for a long moment and said, "Thank you for telling me."

qa.q: What did the manager ask Jahnavi in reply to the Friday email?
qa.a: 'Can you lead the next survey too?'

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when he first saw the slides on Monday?
qa.a: Harish felt a hot flush of anger, but doubted himself and told himself it was a misunderstanding.

qa.q: Which choice finally worked, and why?
qa.a: Booking fifteen minutes with Jahnavi and the manager and showing timestamped drafts; the facts made the claim clear without a fight.

qa.q: How did the manager see things before and after the meeting?
qa.a: Before, the manager believed the work was Jahnavi's and offered her the next survey; after seeing the timestamps, the manager thanked Harish for speaking up.

grounding: Shows an employee whose silence let a colleague's claim on his analysis grow, until he spoke up with evidence.

passage: You asked why I always put my name and the date on the first slide, Gautam. Let me tell you. I was twenty-four, at a cement company in Nagpur, and I spent three weekends building a model of where our trucks wasted fuel. I emailed it to my manager, Mr Kale, on a Monday. On Friday, at the quarterly review, there it was on the big screen, my charts, my colours, even my spelling mistake in Chandrapur, under his name. The directors applauded him. I sat in the back row, face hot. Angry, yes, but mostly doubting myself. Maybe he had improved it? Maybe asking would make me look petty. So I said nothing. Three months later he did it again with my vendor report. My silence had told him it was fine. The second time, I went to his cabin with my dated emails and said calmly, "I'd like my name on this." He was annoyed. It never happened a third time. Your Raghav sir learned it late. Speak the first time.

qa.q: Which word did Raghav misspell in the charts?
qa.a: Chandrapur.

qa.q: Why did Raghav stay silent the first time?
qa.a: Raghav felt angry but mostly doubtful, and afraid that asking would look petty, so stayed silent.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what did Raghav do?
qa.a: After the vendor report was taken too, Raghav went to Mr Kale's cabin with dated emails and calmly asked for his name on the work.

qa.q: How might Mr Kale have read Raghav's silence after the first time?
qa.a: Mr Kale probably took the silence as consent, which is why he did it again with the vendor report.

grounding: Shows an employee finding their work under a manager's name, feeling anger, doubt and fear of seeming petty, whose silence is taken as consent until they speak.
